en: The *Sūtra of the Parable of King Aśoka*, translated by an anonymous author and appended to the catalog of the Eastern Jin dynasty, states:
In ancient times, there was a great king named Aśoka. He ruled over all nations, and there were none who did not submit as his subjects.
The Great King was intelligent and possessed immeasurable wisdom;
he instructed his ministers to inquire:
"Is there anything in the world that does not belong to me?"
The ministers replied,
"The entire world belongs to Your Majesty;
there is none who does not submit."
Among them, a wise minister replied:
"Within Your Majesty's realm, there are those who do not belong to the King;
among them, the Dragon Kings in the ocean do not belong to Your Majesty."
"From the beginning, he has neither sent messengers nor made any offerings;
by this, we know he does not belong to Your Majesty.
Your Majesty may test him."
With a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
they beat the bells and struck the drums;
their banners and standards protected him as he proceeded from front to back until reaching the seashore.
The dragon king remained silent and did not emerge.
The king then called out to him,
saying, "You are within my domain!"
He did not offer an explanation and remained silent, giving no answer to the king.
The king then questioned his wise ministers.
"By what means can the Dragon King be made to emerge?
The wise minister replied,
"He can indeed be made to emerge."
The Dragon King possesses immense merit;
for this reason, he is unwilling to submit.
Great King, if you do not believe my words, [then observe him yourself].
He weighed out two jin of gold to cast two images:
one fashioned as the image of the King,
and the other as the image of the Dragon King.
They weighed them again;
the image of the Dragon King was heavy,
while the image of the Great King was light.
"By this, it is known that the Dragon King possesses great merit while Your Majesty possesses little merit.
The king’s mind was deeply enlightened.
Filled with immeasurable joy,
he issued a decree throughout the realm to provide for the elderly and the orphaned,
and to relieve the destitute and the impoverished.
In the various prefectures and counties, temples for the Celestial Honored One (Tianzun) were established,
and assemblies were convened to enshrine relics of the Celestial Honored One and make offerings to them.
Within three years, they again took the image of the Dragon King and the image of the King of Images and weighed them.
The dragon-king was then slighted,
while the king-king was treated with gravity.
A wise minister addressed the king, saying:
"The dragon may now be subdued.
He then set out with a ceremonial procession as before and returned to the seashore.
There, the Dragon King transformed himself into a young Brahmin.
He knelt for a long time before the king to inquire after his well-being,
presented all the rare treasures and exquisite jewels found in the ocean as tribute,
and declared himself a subject.
The people throughout the land were all filled with joy;
this is recorded separately in the scriptural text to be shown to future generations.
In all the world, there is no strength that surpasses merit and virtue.
If a person protects the sutras and the Dharma as a mother protects her child,
how can one not contemplate this?
Formerly, when the World-Honored One was in the world,
he was teaching and transforming sentient beings with his disciples. Seeing a piece of paper on the ground,
the disciple Ānanda immediately picked it up.
The World-Honored One told Ānanda to release his hand from the ground.
Ānanda immediately released it,
and his hand became exceedingly fragrant.
Proceeding a short distance further, he saw grass being blown by a whirlwind upon the ground.
Ānanda picked it up again,
and the World-Honored One said to Ānanda, "Let it down to the ground."
His hands immediately smelled foul.
Ānanda did not understand;
he thought he would go to the vihāra shortly and inquire about the meaning of this.
Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One:
"By what cause does the hand become fragrant when holding paper,
yet foul-smelling when holding grass?"
The Celestial Honored One said to Ānanda:
"This paper came from the Land of Fragrance;
the fragrance has permeated the paper."
Therefore, your hands are fragrant;
because the grass came from a foul-smelling place,
therefore your hands are foul-smelling.
Associating with the virtuous is like fragrance adhering to paper;
associating with the wicked is like a foul odor adhering to grass.
Therefore, the sutra says: "By associating with the virtuous, one achieves wisdom."
Associating with fools increases one's delusion.
There are three things that harm me,
and three things that benefit me.
This is what is meant by "one must not fail to be careful.
Formerly, when the World-Honored One was with his disciples at the riverbank,
the World-Honored One spoke to the disciples.
He took a stone about the size of a fist and threw it into the water to see whether it would float or sink.
His disciple replied:
The stone sank to the bottom of the water.
The World-Honored One said,
"It is because there is no causal condition."
Furthermore, there was a stone slab, three feet square, which he placed upon the water and crossed the river;
even after he had passed, the stone remained completely dry. How could this be?
The disciples, not yet understanding, were all struck with wonder.
The disciples knelt with their right knees on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By what cause is it thus?
The World-Honored One replied:
It is simply because there are virtuous conditions.
What constitutes these conditions?
The World-Honored One has borrowed the analogy of a boat.
One who encounters a virtuous teacher shall escape from manifold sufferings;
one who encounters an evil teacher [shall not].
Thus, by habituating oneself to evil deeds, one does not escape manifold calamities;
this serves as a warning to people of future generations that they must not fail to exercise caution.
Formerly, there was an old man, impoverished, cold, and solitary,
who had no means to support himself;
he happened upon a marketplace and obtained an axe.
This is the finest of all jewels,
yet he did not recognize it;
he took up his staff and went about selling it.
As I used my axe to exhaust this meager life of mine,
I saw a foreign merchant of great means,
a caravan leader named Sārthavāha.
Recognizing it as an axe,
he asked the old man,
"Will you sell this axe?"
The husband said, "I rely on this axe for my livelihood; I will not sell it.
The merchant spoke again.
He gave me a hundred bolts of silk; why did you not sell them?
The official thought it referred to himself, yet he also did not respond to the jest.
The Sārthavāha spoke again:
"Why do you not accept it?
I shall give two hundred horses to you."
The lord then became despondent and unhappy.
The Sārthavāha spoke again, saying,
"If you find it insufficient, I shall increase it."
"Why do you not rejoice?
I shall give you five hundred horses.
Thereupon, the Duke wept bitterly and said:
"I do not resent the lack of silk.
I am merely foolish that this axe, one foot and five inches long, has already exhausted its cutting power upon the ground;
yet with the remaining five inches, I can still obtain five hundred bolts."
"This is why I feel such regret.
The Sārthavāha spoke again,
"Do not harbor further regrets."
"I now give you a thousand bolts of silk.
He then tore up the contract and took it away,
saying, "This axe is the finest of all precious treasures."
Sābha did not ask how much there was, but placed his axe upon it;
when the firewood was consumed by the flames, it was entirely transformed into precious jewels.
The World-Honored One used this as a metaphor.
Having received a human body with all six sense faculties intact, and being intelligent, wise, and eloquent,
one should approach an enlightened teacher to seek the way to transcend the world; thus,
one may attain supernormal powers.
Yet those who are attached to worldly conventions and cannot distinguish between the true and the false,
employ oxen for plowing and driving them according to the customs of their time;
until they reach old age and death, they shall again undergo punishment for their deeds.
It would be like a lord exhausting his precious axe;
how could that not be a mistake?
Formerly, on the Long Mountains, there was a bird whose name was "parrot."
Passing from place to place, he eventually reached Mount Tai in the East.
Among all the beasts and birds there, there were none who did not revere and love him,
for they had come from afar to meet him.
He was like a dear friend with whom he shared great affection and joy.
When the wild fires of spring burned the forest,
he would enter the water and fly over the flames, shaking the water from his feathers.
He went back and forth more than once to rescue his relatives from their distress. But alas,
how could the tears of a parrot, shed with such piteous cries and great lamentation, ever extinguish a fire?
Sincere devotion moved Heaven to send down rain,
and the fire was immediately extinguished.
The *Tianzun jing* (Scripture of the Celestial Honored One) borrows this event as a metaphor.
The worthy ones, having traveled from afar as practitioners of the Way, refined their essence and practiced the Path.
They reduced their own sustenance for body and mouth, even curtailing the portions of their wives and children, to provide offerings to the assembly of monks.
Although they lacked supernatural powers to move others, [they were nonetheless honored].
Furthermore, by burning incense with utmost sincerity to seek their cessation,
and by performing various prostrations, one shall obtain immeasurable merit;
it is like when rain falls from heaven and all calamities are entirely extinguished.
In the past, there was a great elder whose wealth was immeasurable.
He had a granary containing a thousand *hu* of grain, but when he later went out to retrieve it, the grain was nowhere to be seen;
instead, he saw a small child about three years old who could not yet speak.
The elder did not even know what the name of that letter was;
he placed it by the side of the great road in front of his gate,
yet among the passersby on the path, there were still some who recognized it.
From the east of the house, a carriage approached, drawn by yellow oxen;
the driver wore yellow robes, and his attendants were all dressed in yellow.
Upon passing and seeing the young boy, he spoke.
"Why does this thief of grain sit here?
This child is the deity of the five grains.
He spoke thus to the elder, who then took up a spade.
"Bring an axe.
I will tell you where the basin of gold is.
The one who has just passed by is the deity of gold."
Proceeding west along the road and turning south onto the path,
walk two hundred paces; there,
to the west of the path, there should be a dilapidated old tree.
Beneath it was a jar containing ten *hu* of gold.
"Go there and dig it up; you can use it to repay the value of your grain.
The elder followed the boy's instructions, obtained the treasure, and his household became immensely wealthy.
The Buddhist scriptures borrow this as a metaphor:
to provide offerings to the Sangha by extensively arranging dāna assemblies and incurring great expenses is likened to the loss of grain.
The Daoist preaches the sutras and explains their meaning to teach people to distance themselves from evil and pursue the good.
Only after obtaining immeasurable blessings can one reach the Way;
this may be likened to obtaining a golden basin.
This is shown as instruction for future generations:
one must cultivate merit and virtue;
once regret arises, it will be too late.
In the past, there was a kingdom that was prosperous, peaceful, and free from any lack or want.
He then spoke to his great ministers,
dispatching one minister who was capable of being sent on a mission.
As for those things he did not possess in his own country, he went to other lands to purchase them.
He then dispatched a man to another country, taking with him abundant precious jewels to inspect the various marketplaces; however, there was nothing else to be found.
"All that belongs within my kingdom has been exhausted," he said.
Finally, seeing a worthy man sitting empty-handed upon his stall, he asked him:
"I do not see that you have anything to sell.
Why are you sitting here in vain?
He replied, "I am selling wisdom here."
Question: "What is the appearance of your wisdom, and how much do you ask for it?
He replied:
"My wisdom is worth five hundred taels of gold.
Previously, when you mentioned gold, I intended to explain it to you.
At this, the traveler thought to himself:
In our country, there is no one who sells wisdom to others;
however, having weighed out five hundred taels of gold for that person,
I shall immediately impart to them the words of wisdom.
Regarding these twenty words of instruction:
one should contemplate them with long-term foresight and careful reflection;
one ought not to act impulsively out of anger.
"Though it may not be used today,
there will surely come a time when it is needed.
Thereupon, he received and recited the instructions until they were mastered, and each returned to their respective homes.
Having acquired these words of wisdom, the minister immediately returned to his country, traveling by way of his own home.
Entering at night, he saw two sandals before the bed of Lady Bright Moon;
suspecting the presence of some strange person, he conceived an evil thought.
His wife suddenly fell ill, and his mother went to stay with them.
Seeing that the elder was still speaking words of wisdom without ceasing,
the mother was startled awake and asked, "Has your son returned?"
The child then ran out of the door and called out, "Jianjian!
His mother asked him what he was saying.
He replied, "What have you gained by your actions?"
"Why do you call me base?
the son said. "My mother would not give me away even for ten thousand taels of gold;
yet she now looks at me as if I were worth only five hundred taels—is that not being base?"
The scriptures of the Celestial Honored One borrow [these things] as metaphors;
a single word of popular proverbial wisdom is more beneficial than a thousand pieces of gold.
This is what is meant by that. Formerly,
when the World-Honored One was by the banks of the Ganges River,
he extensively expounded the Dharma of the sutras.
At that time, devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, humans, birds, and beasts all came to listen to the Dharma.
There was an old cowherd who stood leaning on his staff to listen;
he did not notice that there was a frog beneath the staff.
The frog listened to the sutra with such delight that he was unaware of the staff upon his back; consequently,
after a long time, the frog’s life came to an end.
That spirit was immediately reborn in the heavens.
Using his divine eye to observe its origin,
he saw from which path it had come and beheld his former body within a frog.
Heavenly flowers descended upon his former body to manifest this teaching for future generations:
that by listening to the sutra with a focused mind while among frogs, one may attain rebirth in the heavens.
How much more so for a worthy person who listens to the sutra with a sincere heart—
is this not truly magnificent?
Long ago, there were two brothers.
The younger brother went to pursue the enlightened teacher and became a śramaṇa;
he subsequently attained the path of an arhat and came repeatedly to speak with his elder brother.
"You should diligently cultivate merit.
His elder brother replied, "I am currently preoccupied with urgent affairs; I must wait until later."
This occurred not just once, but repeatedly.
Later, when the elder brother passed away,
the younger brother used his eye of the Path to observe the realm in which his brother’s spirit had been reborn.
When one examines the realms of devas and humans, the spirit is not seen therein;
furthermore, when observing the realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts, it is likewise not seen;
it is found instead within the realm of animals.
He saw his elder brother’s spirit transformed into a great ox.
At that time, a merchant was driving the ox for trade when the road became treacherous;
he stumbled into the mud and was unable to rise up by himself.
The merchant struck him with a staff,
yet he still stretched out his throat and did not rise.
When the younger brother saw his elder brother in such a state, [he was overcome with grief].
He came straight up before the ox and said to his elder brother,
"What is this sudden business today? It is quite different from how it was before."
The ox immediately felt shame and grief so profound that it died.
The practitioner departed at once.
The merchants then deliberated together, saying:
"Why has this practitioner come to cast a spell to kill my ox?
he asked, and immediately pursued the practitioner,
bringing him back to interrogate him regarding his intentions and circumstances.
The practitioner explained the matter to him as it was, saying, "The ox is my elder brother;
it was because you did not follow my words that you incurred this transgression.
Thereupon, the practitioner threw his alms bowl into the air.
The bird followed after him.
The merchants, realizing he was a holy man,
then reproached themselves.
By burning incense for the ox and performing meritorious deeds,
one gains the merit to be reborn in the heavens.
Long ago, there was a worthy man.
It is situated thirty *li* southeast of the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
The family observes the Dharma and makes offerings to practitioners of the Way.
However, the head of the household takes pleasure in killing pigs and selling their meat.
The practitioner gradually became aware of this,
but before he could rebuke or admonish him, the old man passed away.
Within the Ganges River, they take the forms of ghosts and spirits;
there are those with iron wheels whose sharp edges are like frost and snow,
which pierce them as they follow the current.
The pain was beyond description.
On a later day, as the practitioner was crossing the Ganges River, he encountered a spirit.
The spirit then emerged with half its body above the water.
The boatman spoke threateningly:
"I will throw this practitioner into the water;
otherwise, I shall kill everyone on board."
At that time, there was a wise man who asked the spirit,
"For what reason do you seek this practitioner?
The spirit replied:
"When I was in the world, I made offerings to practitioners of the Way.
These practitioners knew in their hearts that I slaughtered pigs and sold their meat,
yet they did not rebuke or admonish me."
"Therefore, you have merely killed a practitioner of the Way.
The worthy one then said,
"It is because you sat by the slaughtered pig that you have incurred this retribution."
"Now you wish to kill a practitioner of the Way;
is your sin not indeed great?
The spirit reflected and thought, "It is truly as the worthy one has said."
He then released him to go.
Having departed, the practitioner returned and told his family members and descendants to perform meritorious deeds on his behalf.
The deity was immediately freed from suffering.
He spoke thus to instruct future generations:
"A practitioner who receives offerings must not fail to provide instruction and admonition."
Once, there was a man traveling on a road who saw a dead person lying there;
a spirit was lashing it with a staff.
A traveler asked, "This person is already dead; for what reason do you whip him?
The spirit replied:
This was my former body.
During its lifetime, it was unfilial toward its parents and disloyal toward its sovereign.
I failed to revere the Triple Gem and did not follow the instructions of my teachers;
this has caused me to fall into sinful states of suffering that are difficult to describe.
"It is solely because of my old body that I have come to be whipped.
As he proceeded further, he again saw a dead man upon whose corpse a heavenly deity had descended and scattered flowers.
He rubbed it with his hand.
A traveler asked him,
"I observe that you appear to be a deva."
"Why do you touch this corpse?
He replied, "This was my former body; on the day it was born, I was filial toward my parents."
Serve the sovereign with loyalty and integrity;
revere and honor the Triple Gem;
and receive the teachings of one's preceptor.
That my spirit has been able to attain rebirth in heaven is entirely due to the kindness of my former body;
it is for this reason that I have come to repay it.
One day, the traveler witnessed these two transformations;
he immediately returned home to uphold the five precepts and practice the ten wholesome deeds,
serving his parents with filial piety and attending to his sovereign with loyalty and integrity.
This is shown as instruction for future generations:
merit and demerit follow a person for a long time and do not let go;
one must therefore be cautious.
Long ago, there was a practitioner who was studying the Way in the mountains.
Someone sent a śrāmaṇera to Śrāvastī.
Every day he was required to provide one *dǒu* of rice and was additionally tasked with reciting one verse.
In the marketplace, there was a virtuous man who sat at a stall;
seeing the śrāmaṇera, he spoke with him as they walked along.
He asked the śrāmaṇera,
"As you walk back and forth searching, why do you speak while walking?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"My teacher studies the Way in the mountains.
Daily he demands one *dou* of rice from me and assigns me one verse to recite.
For this reason, I have been reciting one verse at a time."
The worthy one asked again:
"If you do not have to deliver rice, how many verses can you recite by heart?
He replied: "I can recite ten verses by heart."
The worthy one then said,
"Do not go separately again;
I shall personally take the place of the śrāmaṇera to deliver the rice."
The śrāmaṇera was delighted and immediately began his studies in quiet seclusion.
The worthy man provided nine *shu* of rice for the śrāmaṇera;
thereafter, when the śrāmaṇera was tested on the sūtras, he had mastered them all through his own insight.
The worthy one was reborn in a later age as a disciple of the World-Honored One (Tianzun),
named Ānanda. The World-Honored One possessed twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana).
The karmic reward for intelligence cannot be described merely as "knowing ten when one is asked";
it is intended to show future generations that merit and virtue follow the person like a shadow follows a form.
Each person obtains the merit according to what they have sown;
one must not fail to act.
Long ago, there was a butcher who raised a thousand head of cattle, fattening them until they were healthy and well-fed.
He slaughtered one ox every day to sell its meat;
having slaughtered five hundred oxen,
five hundred heads remained.
Just as they were leaping about, frolicking, and butting one another,
the World-Honored One entered the kingdom;
seeing the oxen in such a state, he looked upon them with compassion and departed.
He said to his disciples,
"This ox is foolish;
only when its companions are nearly exhausted does it begin to frolic and clamor."
Human beings are likewise thus.
As each day passes, the lifespan of people diminishes further; one must therefore contemplate and diligently seek the Way that transcends the world.
The Scripture on the Parable of King Aśoka Spoken by the World-Honored One.
